Synergistic co-steam gasification of biomass and refuse-derived fuel: A path to enhanced gasification performance Jianjun Cai  a,b,c* , Lingxia Zhu a , Jianbo Yang  a,* , Minjia Guo  a , Mingkang Fang b , Shengfeng Yao b a School of Architecture and Traffic, Guilin University of Electronic Technology, Guilin 541004, China. b Mizuda Group Co., Ltd., Huzhou 310000, China c National Engineering Laboratory for High-Efficiency Recovery of Refractory Nonferrous Metals, School of Metallurgy and Environment, Central South University, Changsha, 410083, PR China Corresponding authors: Prof. Jianjun Cai, E-mail address: caijianjun@guet.edu.cn A. P. Jianbo Yang, E-mail address: yangjianbo@guet.edu.cn Preprint not peer reviewed

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Abstract: The co-steam gasification of biomass (straw) and Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF) presents a promising  pathway  for  sustainable  waste  management  and  renewable  energy  production,  with significant implications  for  environmental  protection.  This  study  investigates  the  impact  of gasification temperature and steam-to-biomass (S/M) ratio on the process's efficiency, syngas quality, and environmental outcomes. The experiments reveal that optimizing these operational parameters is crucial  for  enhancing  syngas  production-rich  in  hydrogen  (H2)  and  carbon  monoxide  (CO)-while minimizing  the  generation  of  tar  and  other  undesirable  by-products.  An  optimal  S/M  ratio  was identified  that  maximizes  H2  and  CO  yields  and  promotes  tar  conversion  efficiency,  thereby improving the environmental profile of the gasification process. Higher gasification temperatures were found to further increase syngas yield and quality by facilitating mineral transformations and structural changes in the solid residue, thus supporting energy recovery and minimizing environmental hazards. Notably, the co-gasification of RDF and straw exhibited synergistic effects, leading to enhanced syngas yields, improved carbon conversion, and cold gas efficiencies, especially at elevated temperatures and optimal S/M ratios. These synergies, attributed to catalytic interactions between feedstock constituents, result in a gas output with reduced CO2 and CH4 levels, indicative of an optimized energy source. The study underscores the potential of co-steam gasification of straw and  RDF  as  a  technologically  viable  and  environmentally  friendly  approach  to  waste-to-energy conversion, emphasizing the importance of operational optimization for achieving superior energy recovery, resource efficiency, and reduced environmental impact. Keywords: Municipal solid waste; biomass; gasification; syngas; synergistic enhancement. Preprint not peer reviewed

1. Introduction As  the  world  strides  toward  a  more  sustainable  energy  future,  the  integration  of  renewable energy sources has become imperative. Among these, biomass stands out as a prominent, carbonneutral  resource  due  to  its  abundant  availability  and  renewable  nature  [1].  However,  biomass utilization is often hindered by its intrinsic properties, such as low energy density and heterogeneity [2]. Parallel to this, the escalating volumes of municipal solid waste (MSW) have given rise to the generation of refuse-derived fuel (RDF), which encompasses a high-energy-value waste fraction that can be recovered as energy instead of being landfilled [3]. While RDF offers a significant energy recovery option, its gasification is often challenged by the presence of diverse and complex materials [4].  The  steam  co-gasification  of  biomass  and  RDF  presents  a  viable  solution  that  harnesses  the strengths  of  both  feedstocks  while  mitigating  their  individual  limitations  through  synergistic interactions. Synergy in co-gasification processes arises when the interactions between biomass and RDF during gasification lead to improved gas yields, calorific values, and carbon conversion efficiency, as compared to their individual gasification [5]. These benefits are attributed to the complementary properties of the feedstocks. For instance, RDF often contains plastics and other materials with high calorific value that can increase the energy content of the gas product [6]. In contrast, biomass can contribute to the stability of the process with its consistent composition and char-forming ability, which can enhance tar cracking and improve syngas quality [7]. The influence of gasification temperature on the co-gasification of biomass and RDF is a subject of considerable study. Higher temperatures typically enhance the gasification reactions, leading to increased  syngas  yields  and  improved  carbon  conversion  efficiencies  [8].  However,  the  optimal temperature range must be identified to maximize synergetic effects while avoiding excessive thermal degradation of the feedstocks, which could lead to the formation of undesirable byproducts. The S/M ratio plays a pivotal role in the gasification process, influencing the steam reforming of hydrocarbons, water-gas shift reactions, and the overall energy balance of the system [9]. A carefully optimized S/M ratio can promote the production of hydrogen, an essential component of high-quality syngas, and reduce the formation of tars and chars [9]. The determination of the ideal S/M ratio is thus crucial for achieving optimal syngas composition and maximizing the synergetic effects between biomass and Preprint not peer reviewed

RDF.  Analyzing  the  gasification  characteristics  involves  assessing  the  composition  and  calorific value of the syngas produced, as well as the cold gas efficiency, which provides an indication of the overall energy efficiency of the gasification process. Furthermore, the carbon conversion efficiency is a critical parameter, reflecting the effectiveness of the gasification in transforming feedstock carbon into gas-phase products [10]. The characterization of the residual solids from gasification, including their composition and morphology, is equally important. Advanced characterization techniques such as Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) are employed to analyze the solid byproducts. EDS provides elemental composition data, which can inform the understanding of ash behavior and the potential for catalyst activity within the residual solids. SEM offers insights into the physical structure and the morphology of the chars, which can be correlated with reactivity and gasification dynamics [11]. Therefore, the synergy in co-gasification is not just a theoretical concept but also a practical approach  to  optimize  the  energy  output  from  available  resources.  The  combined  gasification characteristics, such as syngas composition, thermal value, cold gas efficiency, and carbon conversion efficiency, provide a comprehensive picture of the process performance. Moreover, the physicochemical analysis of the gasification residues through EDS and SEM further elucidates the transformation mechanisms during co-gasification, shedding light on the intricate interplays at work. This study aims to systematically investigate the individual and combined effects of gasification temperature and S/M ratio on the co-gasification of biomass and RDF. By analyzing the process outputs and residue characteristics, we seek to optimize the gasification parameters for enhanced synergetic effects, leading to the production of high-quality syngas and the efficient utilization of solid residues. The outcomes of this research will have implications for the design and operation of co-gasification systems, potentially contributing to a more sustainable and effective waste-to-energy conversion technology. 2. Experimental 2.1. Characteristics of biomass and RDF The straw and refuse-derived fuel (RDF) utilized in the experimental procedures of this study have  been  sourced  consistent  with  the  feedstock  characteristics  reported  in  our  team's  prior Preprint not peer reviewed

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

publications [12]. Detailed compositional and proximate analyses, alongside industrial characterizations of the biomass and RDF, have been extensively documented in these previous works. For  a  comprehensive  understanding  of  the  feedstock  properties,  readers  are  referred  to  these foundational studies [12]. This established baseline of knowledge has been instrumental in informing the  experimental  design  and  facilitating  a  deeper  interpretation  of  the  gasification  characteristics observed in the present study. 2.2. Examples of biomass and RDF steam gasification Investigations into the co-steam gasification of RDF and straw were conducted using a fixedbed laboratory reactor, as depicted in Scheme 1 . The procedure commenced with nitrogen at a flow rate  of  3L/min,  constituting  5%  of  the  total  flow  to  serve  as  the  carrier  gas  for  the  steam.  Upon reaching the pre-set temperature of 220°C by the heating belt, the steam generator was activated. The liquid  pump was then engaged at various speeds (S/M=0.25, 0.50, 0.75, or 1.00) and allowed to stabilize the steam flow. A constant total gas flow rate of 150 mL/min was maintained to negate the influence of flow rate variations on gasification outcomes. Experimental samples weighing 2 g and having a particle size of 0.075 mm, were placed in an alumina crucible at the reactor's entrance. Nitrogen at 150 mL/min was introduced for 20 minutes to purge the reactor of residual air. The reactor's heating rate was set at 15 °C/min until reaching the target temperatures of 600°C, 700°C, 800°C, or 900°C. The crucible was then repositioned to the reactor's center for a 20-minute duration. Syngas was cooled in a water bath to remove tar and moisture. Given that the majority of syngas was produced  within  the  initial  10  minutes,  it  was  captured  in  sampling  bags  during  this  interval. Subsequent gases were combusted. Tar and dry syngas were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC  model  3420A,  Beijing  Beifen-Ruili  Analytical  Instrument  Group  Co.,  Ltd).  Each  sample underwent triplicate testing, with the mean value recorded as the final result. Preprint not peer reviewed

Scheme 1. Diagram of the laboratory scale fixed-bed reactor facility. The  volume  fraction  of  the  syngas  ( Vi ),  the  volume  yield  of  the  syngas  composition  ( YG,  i , Nm 3 /kg),  the  LHV  of  syngas  (MJ/kg),  the  carbon  conversion  efficiency  (CC),  and  the  cold  gas efficiency (CGE) were calculated based on the related equations in our previous report [12]. Previous studies  indicated  that  co-gasification  processes  incorporating  40-50%  MSW  (or  RDF)  yield satisfactory results. Consequently, we employed a 1:1 mass ratio of RDF to straw as the feedstock for co-gasification in our study [13-15]. 2.3. Characterization Sample  compositions  were  characterized  by  X-ray  diffraction  (XRD)  using  a  D/max2400 instrument  (Rigaku  Corporation,  Japan).  Microstructural  analysis  was  conducted  with  a  field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM; Gemini SEM 500, Zeiss, Germany). Elemental analysis was performed on the same FE-SEM model, which was outfitted with an Oxford energydispersive spectrometer (EDS). 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Characteristics of biomass gasification Fig. 1 comprehensively examines the effects of varying steam-to-mass of biomass (S/M) ratios on the gasification characteristics of straw. Fig. 1a manifests the direct relationship between S/M ratio and  gas  composition.  Notably,  an  optimal  S/M  ratio  seems  to  maximize  H2  and  CO  yields,  key components of syngas, which is desirable for conversion to liquid fuels or power generation. This is coherent with the enhanced reforming and water-gas shift reactions reported in contemporary studies Preprint not peer reviewed

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

focused  on  biomass  gasification  [16].  Furthermore,  the  diminishing  outputs  of  CO2,  CH4,  and hydrocarbons with increasing S/M ratios may signal a shift in the reaction pathways towards those favoring syngas production over carbon reformation as described by Shim et al.[5]. Fig. 1b reveals an inverse relationship between the LHV and the S/M ratio, with a concomitant increase in the H2/CO ratio. This indicated that an increase in steam availability relative to biomass facilitates tar cracking and reforming, thus enriching the hydrogen content in the produced gas. Fig. 1c relates carbon conversion efficiency and cold gas efficiency to the S/M ratio. The carbon conversion efficiency measures the extent to which carbonaceous matter in the straw is transformed into  gaseous  constituents  [17],  whereas  the  cold  gas  efficiency  provides  an  indication  of  the  net calorific value of the gas produced relative to the straw input [18]. The non-linear effects of S/M ratios on carbon conversion and cold gas efficiency were depicted. A discernible vertex suggested an optimal S/M ratio, beyond which the further addition of steam leads to a reduction in efficiency, possibly attributable to the saturation of reactive sites or heat consumption by excess steam. Fig. 1d compares the by-product yield distributions, including tar, solids, and gas, across varying S/M ratios of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0. Tar production minimization is a critical target in gasification processes, as  high  tar  levels  can  lead  to  downstream  equipment  fouling.  The  decreasing  trend  of  tar  with increasing S/M ratios was consistent with the hypothesis of enhanced tar cracking under steam-rich conditions, an observation in line with recent studies that advocate for steam-enabled tar reduction strategies [19]. The  relationship  between temperature and efficiency metrics such as carbon conversion and cold gas efficiency was depicted in Fig. 2c. Both efficiencies increased with temperature, indicating a complete conversion of straw into syngas and a higher relative calorific value of the syngas produced. These trends illustrated that operating at elevated temperatures could enhance overall energy recovery from straw gasification. Preprint not peer reviewed

Characteristics of RDF gasification In  the  pursuit  of  sustainable  waste  management,  optimizing  the  S/M  ratio  is  critical  for enhancing resource recovery through steam gasification while mitigating the environmental impact. A lower S/M ratio exhibited higher concentrations of CO and H2, as indicated in Fig. 5a, which is desirable for syngas production. However, as shown in Fig. 5b, lower S/M ratios increased gas yield. Conversely, a higher S/M ratio demonstrated reduced tar production and an increase in tar conversion efficiency, aligning with the goal of waste-harmless disposal by minimizing the output of harmful byproducts. Moreover, the inflection points in Fig. 5c suggest a threshold beyond which additional steam does not significantly enhance the gasification process but affects the thermal efficiency, as corroborated by the reduction in cold gas efficiency at higher S/M ratios. In Fig. 5a, we can observe the influence of the S/M ratio on the synthesis gas component yields. Higher ratios appear to increase the yield of H2 and CO, which is favorable for syngas applications such as energy recovery and chemical synthesis, due to their high combustion energy and chemical reactivity, respectively. This is consistent with the promotion of the steam reforming and water-gas Preprint not peer reviewed

shift reactions at elevated steam concentrations, leading to enhanced H2 production. Conversely, CO2 and light hydrocarbon gases like CH4 and C2H4 display a decrease in yield with higher S/M ratios. The reduction in CO2 yield could possibly be explained by a shift in the Boudouard reaction towards the  production  of  CO,  while  the  suppression  of  CH4  and  C2H4  suggests  the  advancement  of hydrocarbon cracking and reforming pathways with an increase in steam supply. The impact of the S/M ratio on the syngas yield and its lower heating value is presented in Fig. 5b. The syngas yield shows a negative correlation with the S/M ratio, indicating that past a certain point, additional steam does not contribute to increasing the yield, likely due to the dilution effect or energy losses from the endothermic steam gasification reaction. This is accompanied by a reduction in LHV, likely reflecting an increase in non-combustible gas fractions and a diluted energy content of the syngas. Fig. 5c offers insights into the process efficiency, illustrated by the changes in carbon conversion and  cold  gas  efficiency  across  different  S/M  ratios.  Both  metrics  exhibit  pronounced  peaks  at intermediate S/M ratios, after which the efficiency decreases, suggesting an optimal S/M ratio for achieving maximum process efficiency. This optimal point represents a balance between sufficient steam availability for promoting desirable gasification reactions and the avoidance of energy losses due to the excess steam acting as a thermal ballast, diluting the syngas. Finally, Fig. 5d elucidates the variation in the relative distribution of tar, solid, and gaseous products. As the S/M ratio increases, tar production significantly decreases, likely due to enhanced tar reforming reactions in the presence of steam. The consistent production of solid byproducts across varying S/M ratios suggests that steam does not significantly affect the yield of solid residues, while the proportion of gas products largely increases, emphasizing the role of steam in driving the gasification reaction towards a more complete conversion of solid waste into gaseous fuels. The interplay between the S/M ratio and these different gasification  outcomes  highlights  the  complexity  of  optimizing  RDF  gasification  processes.  It underscores the need for a careful balance to maximize syngas quality and minimize byproducts while ensuring high carbon conversion and process efficiency. Preprint not peer reviewed

Fig.  6a  shows  the  impact  of  temperature  on  the  composition  of  syngas  produced  from RDF gasification.  The  positive  correlation  between  temperature  and  the  yields  of  H2  and  CO  can  be attributed to enhanced endothermic reactions such as steam reforming and partial oxidation at higher temperatures.  This  results  in  the  thermal  cracking  of  organic  macromolecules  within  the  waste, producing  a  richer  hydrogen  content,  as  higher  temperatures  favor  the  disassociation  of  water molecules in the steam reforming process. Additionally, the decrease in CH4 and C2H4 with increasing temperature may indicate secondary reactions where these species are consumed to generate more H2 and CO. Fig. 6b presents the influence of temperature on both the syngas production rate and its LHV. There  is  an  apparent  enhancement  in  the  production  rate  with  temperature,  suggesting  that  the gasification reactions become more effective at higher thermal conditions. Contrarily, the LHV of the produced syngas increases modestly with temperature, potentially due to the improved quality of the syngas with a higher ratio of combustible gases (H2 and CO) over incombustible ones (CO2 and Preprint not peer reviewed

The variation of carbon conversion and cold gas efficiency with temperature in Fig. 6c further accentuates the importance of thermal conditions in optimizing gasification performance. Carbon conversion  efficiency  increases  with  temperature,  signifying  that  a  higher  fraction  of  the  RDF's carbonaceous content is effectively transformed into gaseous products. This result is concurrent with the rising trend of cold gas efficiency, which is a direct measure of the chemical energy of the syngas compared to the energy input from the RDF. A higher efficiency indicates a more effective conversion of waste to energy. Fig. 6d provides insight into the temperature influence on the relative distribution of tar, solid, and gaseous products. Higher temperatures considerably reduce tar formation, likely due to  thermal  cracking  processes  that  break  down  complex  organic  compounds.  The  ratio  of  solid byproducts  decreases  as  well,  while  the  gas  fraction  augments,  indicating  a  shift  towards  more complete gasification with temperature escalation. compositions. Fig. 7 shows the evolutionary behaviors of the EDS data of the bottom RDF ash for different temperatures at an ER of 0.2. The characterization of solid residues following RDF steam gasification is crucial for understanding the thermal transformation properties and for developing efficient waste management practices. In Fig. 7a, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the solid by-products at different temperatures revealed that the crystallinity and phase composition of the residues evolves with temperature. Specifically, peaks corresponding to salts such as KCl and CaCO3 diminish with increasing  temperature,  indicating  thermal  decomposition  and  potential  volatilization  of  these components. At higher temperatures (e.g., T=900°C), the emergence of new phases, like Ca2SiO4, suggests a reformation of inorganic constituents, which may have implications for the safe disposal and stabilization of the remaining ash. Coupled with the elemental composition analysis in Fig. 7b, the trends observed underscore significant temperature-driven changes in the distribution of major elements within the solid residue. For instance, the concentrations of volatile elements such as Na and K decrease with temperature, corroborating findings by Deng et al. [20] on the volatility of alkali metals during gasification. The retention of heavy metals, such as Ca and Fe, presents opportunities for resource recovery while necessitating strategies for the containment of such elements to prevent leaching and environmental contamination. Fig. 8, illustrate a clear morphological transition from relatively intact fibrous structures to a more amorphous  and  agglomerated  state.  This  result  indicated  that  increasing  temperature  during gasification  leads  to  enhanced  thermal  decomposition  of  organic  components  and  facilitates  the agglomeration of inorganic matter. At the lower temperature of 600°C, the SEM image suggests preservation of the original textural features of RDF, with fibers recognizable, reflecting limited thermal degradation (Fig. 8a). As the temperature increased to 700°C (Fig. 8b) and 800°C (Fig. 8c), progressive morphological changes manifest, characterized by significant deformation and partial melting of the inorganic constituents, indicative of the onset of ash sintering. Finally, at 900°C (Fig. 8d), the SEM analysis demonstrates a nearly  complete  morphological  transformation  into  a  glass-like  structure,  pointing  towards  a substantial viscous flow and sintering of the inorganic materials. These microstructural changes have implications for both the resource recovery potential and the environmental impact of the gasification process.  The  increased  sintering  at  higher  temperatures  could  result  in  decreased  porosity  and increased  leachability  of  toxic  elements  from  the  solid  residues,  suggesting  more  rigorous  posttreatment  procedures  may  be  necessary  for  safe  disposal.  The  SEM  characterizations  provide invaluable insight into optimizing gasification parameters to maximize energy recovery from RDF while minimizing potential environmental hazards of the resulting solid by-products. Characteristics of the co-gasification of RDF and straw Fig. 9a graphically illustrates how the syngas composition depends on the S/M ratio, evidencing a general increase in the generation of H2 and CO, the two major energy carriers in syngas, with higher S/M ratios. This trend is attributable to the improved steam reforming reaction kinetics and intensified water-gas shift reactions at elevated steam inputs. The decrease in the production of CO2 and CH4 with increasing S/M ratio hints at the shifting of reaction equilibria towards the production of H2 and CO, which positions the gas output as a more efficient energy source. The variations in the levels  of  CH4  and  higher  hydrocarbons  like  C2H4  further  suggest  enhanced  cracking  of  heavier hydrocarbons at higher steam inputs, optimizing gas yield for subsequent energy applications. Fig. 9b, on the other hand, reveals a non-linear relation between the S/M ratio and both the syngas yield and  LHV.  The  syngas  yield  peaks  at  a  certain  S/M  ratio,  beyond  which  it  sees  a  downturn, underpinning the concept of an optimum steam input for the gasification process. The decline in LHV alongside increasing S/M ratios manifests the dilution effect excessive steam has within the gas phase, lowering  the  combustible  gas  concentration  and  thus  the  overall  energy  content  available  for Preprint not peer reviewed

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

exploitation. Furthermore, Fig. 9c elucidates the influence of the S/M ratio on carbon conversion and cold gas efficiency.  An  ideal  S/M  ratio  is  designated  by  the  apex  of  the  plots,  which  corresponds  to  a maximization in the carbon conversion-reflecting the successful transformation of the carbonaceous material  in  the  waste  mix  into  a  gas  efficiency-an  indicator  of  the  process's  efficacy  in  turning feedstock  into  valuable  energy.  Lastly,  as  demonstrated  in  Fig.  9d,  adjusting  the  S/M  ratio significantly affects the ratio of tar to solid and gaseous products, with a remarkable decrease in undesirable  tar  production  at  high  S/M  ratios.  Consequently,  elevating  the  S/M  ratio  proves advantageous in augmenting the purity and quality of the gas products, widening their potential for energy recovery applications. temperatures, signifying improved thermal decomposition and gas reforming reactions. Enhancement of these components at elevated temperatures can be linked to the effective breakdown of organic compounds  within  the  waste  mixture,  underlining  the  endothermic  nature  of  steam  gasification reactions which mobilize carbon into energy-rich gaseous forms. Conversely, the diminishing yields of CO2 and hydrocarbon gases such as CH4 suggest a favorable shift towards the production of more valuable syngas constituents with higher calorific potential. In Fig. 10b, the syngas yield and LHV trends indicate that the production rate of syngas climbs with temperature, suggesting that the higher energy  input  facilitates  more  efficient  waste  conversion.  The  accompanying  rise  in  LHV  with temperature  confirms  that  such  syngas  have  a  greater  energetic  concentration,  underscoring  the potential  for  enhanced  energy  recovery  from  the  bio-waste  mixture.  This  result  demonstrates  the necessity  of  optimizing  the  temperature  to  maximize  the  output  of  calorific  gases  for  energy applications. Fig. 10c expounds on the effects of temperature on both carbon conversion efficiency and cold gas efficiency, pivotal metrics in judging the performance of gasification. Increment in temperature correlates with higher carbon conversion efficiency, indicating a more complete metamorphosis of the feedstock's carbon into gaseous fuels. The cold gas efficiency, which represents the energetic efficiency of converting feedstock into usable syngas, displays a similarly positive relationship with temperature, reflecting the increased quality of energy obtainable from the waste by thermochemical means.  Fig.  10d  elucidates  the  distribution  of  byproducts  -  tar,  solids,  and  gas  outputs.  Higher operational  temperatures  substantially  reduce  tar  formation,  which  is  beneficial  for  the  gasifier's operation  and  syngas  cleansing  steps.  In  contrast,  the  increase  in  the  gas  fraction  at  higher temperatures promotes the overall goal of energy recovery, while solid residues decrease, signifying a more comprehensive waste-to-energy conversion. Observations  from  Fig.  12a  show  the  solid  residue  at  600°C  with  well-preserved  lamellar structures and fibrous integrity, indicating a lower degree of thermal degradation. The stratified layers are characteristic of cellulose and hemicellulose, components of straw, that have undergone initial thermal attack but retain much of their original structure. Elevating the temperature to 700°C, as shown in Fig. 12b, leads to a noticeable change in the char morphology. The appearance of more fragmented  and  less  defined  structures  suggests  a  higher  degree  of  decomposition.  The  fibrous elements  show  signs  of  disintegration,  which  correlates  with  the  ongoing  devolatilization  and conversion of the organic matter. This intermediate state reflects a transition where increased porosity may enhance the accessibility of reactive sites, thereby facilitating further gasification reactions. At 800°C and 900°C, Fig. 12c and Fig. 12d respectively, there is a clear progression towards a more granular and amorphous char structure. The thermal decomposition is so advanced that the stratification  is  no  longer  visible,  and  the  porosity  has  increased  significantly.  At  the  highest temperature  of  900°C,  the  residue  exhibits  extensive  sintering  with  glassy  surface  morphology, indicating the near completion of organic matter removal and the formation of largely inorganic ash. Higher temperatures promote the agglomeration and fusion of ash particles, creating large voids and a  potentially  vitrified  surface,  which  implies  a  substantial  alteration  in  the  chemical  and  physical properties of the residues. The SEM images delineate the progressive structural changes in RDF and straw residues at escalating temperatures of 600°C (a), 700°C (b), 800°C (c), and 900°C (d) during gasification. 3.4 Synergistic effects from the co-gasification of RDF and straw To quantify the synergistic effects of MSW and straw during gasification, the synergistic effects were calculated using the following formula: ΔM = XcMc + XbMb, where Xc and Xb represent the mass fractions of the feedstocks with types straw and RDF, respectively, and Mc and Mb represent the values of gas yield and carbon conversion efficiency of types straw and RDF, respectively. The synergistic effects based on percentage were calculated using the following formula: SEBP = (Ma ΔM)/ Ma × 100, where ΔM and Ma represent the synergistic effects and the tested values, respectively. In the realm of thermochemical conversion technologies, the steam gasification of municipal solid waste (MSW) has emerged as a pivotal process in sustainable waste management and renewable energy production. The integration of biomass as a co-gasification material with MSW can introduce substantial  synergistic  effects,  as  evidenced  by  the  experimental  outcomes  encapsulated  in  the Preprint not peer reviewed

presented data. These outcomes demonstrate enhanced syngas yields, carbon conversion efficiency, and cold gas efficiency at elevated temperatures. These findings bear significant implications for the advancement of gasification technology, with specific application value in the context of enhanced resource recovery and environmental sustainability. Within the scope of process intensification, the observed synergistic gas yield (Gy) at varying temperatures and S/M ratios elucidates the alterations in reaction dynamics, potentially attributed to the catalytic interactions between the alkali and alkaline earth metallic species inherent to biomass and  the  various  organic  and  inorganic  constituents  of  MSW.  These  interactions  may  lower  the activation  energy  for  key  gasification  reactions,  thereby  facilitating  an  augmented  production  of syngas  that  surpasses  the  outputs  predicted  by  classical  equilibrium  models  predicted  based  on independent behavior of the feedstock constituents. The application value of the increased syngas yield within an industrial context is twofold; firstly, it leads to an elevated generation of a valuable chemical feedstock for the synthesis of liquid fuels and chemicals via subsequent Fischer-Tropsch synthesis or methanol production pathways., Secondly, it provides a higher energy content gas stream compatible for direct utilization in internal combustion engines or turbines for electricity generation, thereby contributing to the displacement of fossil fuelderived energy sources. Carbon conversion efficiency is a vital metric in evaluating the effectiveness of waste-to-energy conversion processes. The increased CC rates underpin the catalytic effect of the ash content within the biomass, which may act to facilitate the gasification of recalcitrant carbon structures present in MSW. This higher conversion rate denotes a more complete utilization of the carbonaceous materials within the waste stream, minimizing the production of undesirable by-products such as tars and chars that can  compromise  process  efficiency  and  generate  disposal  challenges.  From  a  lifecycle perspective,  the  near-complete  carbon  conversion  minimizes  the  carbon  footprint  of  the  waste valorization  process,  making  it  an  attractive  proposition  for  municipalities  striving  towards  zerowaste initiatives. Moreover, the positive deviation in CGE from theoretical expectations underscores the highquality nature of the syngas produced, which is enriched with hydrogen and carbon monoxide, while being low in diluents such as nitrogen, thereby presenting a high heating value. The elevated CGE implies enhanced thermal efficiency of the gasification system and signifies a potential reduction in Preprint not peer reviewed

In conclusion, the synergistic effects manifesting in the co-gasification of MSW with biomass underpin the significant potential for this process in terms of improved efficiency, environmental compatibility, and economic viability. The enhanced performance parameters observed in experimental settings highlight the need for the optimization of process conditions and feedstock compositions  to  realize  the  full  potential  of  this  technology.  The  deployment  of  such  optimized gasification  systems  can  significantly  contribute  to  the  development  of  a  sustainable  waste management infrastructure that aligns with contemporary energy policy objectives aimed at reducing reliance on non-renewable energy sources and mitigating the environmental impact of waste disposal. Conclusions In this investigation, the aim was to assess the individual and combined effects of gasification temperature and S/M ratio on the co-steam gasification of biomass and RDF. These experiments confirmed that the optimal S/M ratios enhance syngas quality by maximizing H2 and CO yields while reducing tar and other by-products in the steam gasification of straw. Increasing temperatures further promote syngas production, as evidenced by higher H2 and CO levels and improved gas yields and efficiencies.  Solid  residue  analyses  confirm  temperature-dependent  mineral  transformations  and structural changes, supporting the optimization of gasification conditions for better energy recovery and environmental compliance. The optimization of the S/M ratio and gasification temperature is crucial for efficient RDF gasification. Lower S/M ratios enhance syngas (CO and H2) production, yet Preprint not peer reviewed

higher ratios reduce tar and increase tar conversion efficiency. The optimal S/M ratio and temperature balance  syngas  yield,  quality  (LHV),  and  process  efficiency  (carbon  conversion  and  cold  gas efficiency),  while  minimizing  environmental  hazards  from  solid  residues.  Temperature  elevation promotes  syngas  production  and  quality,  reduces  tar  and  solid  by-products,  influencing  residue crystallinity and morphology. The investigation into the co-gasification of RDF and straw reveals notable synergies that enhance syngas yield, carbon conversion efficiency, and cold gas efficiency, particularly at elevated temperatures and optimal S/M ratios. These synergistic effects are attributed to catalytic interactions between feedstock constituents, leading to a gas output that is rich in H2 and CO, with reduced levels of CO2 and CH4, indicating an optimized energy source. The optimal S/M ratio and temperature conditions facilitate the maximization of carbon conversion and the efficiency of the gasification process, thereby reducing the production of undesirable by-products such as tar. Additionally, the increased gas yield and energy content of the syngas highlight the potential of this technology for sustainable waste management and renewable energy production. This process not only enhances the efficiency and environmental compatibility of waste-to-energy conversion but also supports the advancement of gasification technology for improved resource recovery and reduced environmental impact.
